**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me he was leaving. He sat at the kitchen table, hands wrapped around a chipped mug of coffee gone cold, and said, *"I can’t do this anymore."* Just five words, but they pressed down on my chest like a stack of encyclopedias. I was eight. I didn’t know then that some sentences are boulders, that they can crush the shape of a life before it’s fully formed.

Words are supposed to be light, aren’t they? They float in the air, dissolve into silence, get lost in the hum of the world. But the heavy ones—they don’t disappear. They sink into your bones. They become part of the architecture of you.

II.

I used to collect words like other kids collected rocks or baseball cards. I’d write them down in a notebook with a blue plastic cover: *serendipity, ephemeral, saudade*. Words that sounded like magic spells, like if I said them just right, I could bend the world to my will. I thought if I knew enough of them, I could build a fortress, a shield against the ones that hurt.

But language is a tricky thing. It’s both weapon and wound. You can say *"I love you"* and mean it with your whole soul, and still, the person hearing it might only feel the weight of what you’re *not* saying. The silences between words are just as heavy as the words themselves.

III.

There’s a myth—I don’t remember where I heard it—that if you speak a person’s true name, you have power over them. Maybe that’s why we’re so careful with the words we use for ourselves. *Depressed. Broken. Unlovable.* Say them too many times, and they start to feel like truth. Say them enough, and they *become* truth.

I spent years calling myself *lost*. It was easier than admitting I was afraid. Easier than saying, *"I don’t know how to be okay."* But words are seeds, too. Plant them deep enough, and they grow into the shape of your life.

IV.

I had a professor in college who said, *"The most dangerous words are the ones we don’t question."* She was talking about propaganda, about the way language can be used to manipulate, to erase. But I think about that in smaller moments, too. The way we say *"I’m fine"* when we’re not. The way we call a war *"a conflict"* to make it sound less brutal. The way we say *"boys will be boys"* and excuse the unexcusable.

Words can be a kind of violence. They can also be a kind of salvation.

V.

I wrote my first real poem when I was sixteen. It was terrible—full of clichés and melodrama—but for the first time, I felt like I had taken the chaos inside me and shaped it into something. It wasn’t pretty, but it was *mine*. That’s the thing about writing: it’s a way to carry the weight without letting it break you. You set the words down on the page, and for a little while, you don’t have to hold them all by yourself.

VI.

I think about the words I’ve swallowed. The *"I miss you"* I didn’t send. The *"I’m sorry"* I couldn’t say. The *"help me"* that stuck in my throat. There’s a kind of silence that’s not empty, but full—full of all the things we’re too afraid to voice.

What would happen if we let them out? Would the world tilt? Would we?

VII.

My mother used to tell me, *"Words are free. It’s how you use them that costs you."* She was right, but I don’t think she realized how expensive they could be. Some words cost you friendships. Some cost you love. Some cost you pieces of yourself you can’t get back.

But here’s the secret: the right words can also buy you freedom. A well-placed *"no"* can be a prison break. A whispered *"yes"* can be a resurrection.

VIII.

I’ve been thinking a lot about the word *"home."* It’s supposed to be a place, but really, it’s a feeling. Or maybe it’s a person. Or maybe it’s just a word we use to describe the absence of longing. I don’t know. I’m still trying to figure out what it means to me.

IX.

There’s a Japanese word: *komorebi*. It means the sunlight that filters through the leaves of trees. Isn’t that beautiful? That there’s a word for something so specific, so fleeting? It makes me wonder how many things we experience every day that don’t have names. How many feelings we carry that we can’t quite articulate.

Maybe that’s why we write. Why we talk. Why we sing. We’re all just trying to name the unnamed.

X.

I used to believe that if I could just find the *right* words, I could fix everything. That if I could string together the perfect sentence, I could mend a broken heart, stop a war, make someone stay. But words aren’t magic. They’re just tools. And like any tool, they’re only as good as the hands that wield them.

XI.

I’m 1,000 words in now, and I don’t have a grand conclusion. No neat bow to tie this up with. Just this: words matter. They shape us, save us, cut us, heal us. They’re the closest thing we have to magic in this world.

So use them carefully. And when you can’t find the right ones, remember that silence is a word, too.

And sometimes, it’s the heaviest one of all.
